standard.title: Features indicate text purpose
standard.description: discuss different texts and identify some features that indicate their purposes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify some familiar texts such as stories and informative texts and their purposes (AC9EFLY01). They have not yet identified specific textual features — language, layout, structural elements — as indicators of purpose.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss different texts and identify features that indicate their purposes.

nodes.label: Texts have purposes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name the purpose of familiar texts and explain how they know.
nodes.minimum_width: State the purpose of at least two different texts and give a reason (e.g. 'it's a story because it has characters and events').
nodes.typical_width: Name and explain the purposes of a range of familiar texts — to entertain, inform, instruct, persuade — with reasons grounded in text features.
wider: Discuss texts that serve more than one purpose simultaneously
Compare how the same information might be presented in texts with different purposes (e.g. a report vs an advertisement)
success_criteria: Student correctly names the purpose of two different texts
Student gives a feature-based reason for each identification

nodes.label: Features signal purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific features of texts — language, layout, structural elements — and explain how each signals the text's purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two features in a given text and explain how each indicates what the text is trying to do.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss features that indicate purpose across a range of text types — headings and diagrams (informative), character names and events (narrative), numbered steps (procedural), opinion language (persuasive).
wider: Compare two texts with different purposes side by side, identifying the distinct features that mark each
Examine digital texts and identify which features indicate purpose in online versus print contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise narrative features as purpose signals cannot classify informative, procedural or persuasive texts in subsequent work — the feature-to-purpose link must be established across multiple text types before any downstream text-type analysis is possible.

response_modes.reason: Students need to see features functioning as purpose signals across varied text types to generalise the concept. Encountering only narrative features risks students equating all text features with storytelling.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing features across multiple text types and considering how features work differently in digital contexts gives advancing students substantive analytical work that builds transferable text literacy.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two features and links each to the text's purpose
Student uses feature-based language ('the headings tell me it's trying to inform')
